newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ex-Irish PM Haughey apologises over cash gift.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Irish PM Haughey apologises over cash gift.

text.p: Former Prime Minister Charles Haughey apologised on Tuesday for misleading an official tribunal over a million-pound gift from a chain store tycoon in a scandal shaking Ireland's political establishment.

Haughey delivered the apology to a tribunal investigating how and why businessman Ben Dunne gave away millions to major political figures including the autocratic three-times prime minister, famous for his lavish lifestyle.
The former premier said he was sorry for previously denying, through his lawyers, that he had received 1.3 million pounds ($2 million) from Dunne between 1989 and 1992.

Dunne has told the tribunal he visited Haughey's north Dublin mansion and handed over cheques for a quarter of a million. "Here's something for yourself," he recalled telling one of the most powerful politicians in modern Irish history.
But Haughey, last in power from 1987 to 1992, said he had "no recollection" of any such incident.
The 71-year-old, never publicity-shy when in power, slipped into Dublin Castle shortly after dawn to avoid photographers and hundreds of members of the public who queued for scant seats.

Wearing a charcoal grey suit, the grey-haired one-time kingmaker, known to friend and foe as "The Boss", said that his financial affairs had been handled by his former partner in an accountancy firm, the late Des Traynor.

He said Traynor, "widely regarded as a financial expert of exceptional ability", had complete control of his money from the 1960s onwards, including the period during which Dunne said he made the payments.

"He saw it as his personal responsibility to ensure that I would be free to devote my time and ability to public life and that I would not be distracted from my political work by financial concerns," said Haughey, making his first appearance before the tribunal.
"Traynor had total discretion to act on my behalf without reference to me. In hindsight, it is clear that I should have involved myself to a greater degree in this regard."

Haughey's admissions have prompted calls for a new tribunal to investigate his financial affairs, an investigation by the tax authorities, and wider calls for new laws governing links between politicians and business.
Haughey said Dunne had not asked for political favours and none had been given. Dunne told the tribunal this year that he had given Haughey money because he had acute financial problems.

The tribunal was set up last year following media reports of mysterious payments to politicians. Michael Lowry, then transport minister, was forced to resign after admitting that Dunne paid for the renovation and extension of his private home.
The panel has heard evidence from all major political parties of huge donations by Dunne for campaign expenses and election funding.
There has been no suggestion by Dunne or the tribunal that political favours were asked for or bought. Dunne testified that he was merely using a personal fortune to help those involved.
The tribunal hearings have been adjourned until next week.

The Dunnes Stores chain owns green-fronted department stores in every town and city of Ireland and is controlled by family members who dropped Ben Dunne from the business five years ago after he was caught by Florida police with a call girl and cocaine.
